stimuli.text: A block of mass 4 kg on a 30° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 6 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.1. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 1.4 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.05\cos(9t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A hoop (I = MR²) and a solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 0.7 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 480 kg load 26 m at constant speed in 30 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: P = W/t.
Correct. P = mgh/t.
Include g.
That is the work; divide by time.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 20 N/m and 90 N/m are connected in series and support a 1.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Both springs share the load.
The force is the weight, mg.
Correct. k_eq = k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).
Series and parallel rules are reversed.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 40° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction acts up the slope.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 5x^3$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 2$$ m to $$x = 3$$ m?

options.why: Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
The force is not constant.

questions.stem: A 0.9 kg ball hits a wall at 18 m/s and rebounds at 10 m/s. The contact lasts 0.06 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Include the rebound.
Divide by time.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 9.5 m high at 14 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Take the square root for the time.
Fall time is √(2h/g).

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 190 m wide, moving at 6 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 3 m/s. How far downstream does the boat land?

options.why: Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
That is a time, not a distance.
Use the crossing time w/v_boat.
Drift = current speed × crossing time.

questions.stem: A 2 kg ball on a 0.4 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 9 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Centripetal force uses v².
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Include gravity.
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -9x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.
T = 2π/ω.
Correct. ω = √9 = 3 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.
ω is the square root of the coefficient.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 39 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 20 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
Recheck the average.
The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 4x^3 - 30x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Take the square root.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 12x² − 30 = 0 gives x = 1.58 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A 7 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 6 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Friction opposes the motion.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Include friction on the table block.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 4 kg and radius 0.6 m spins at 14 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1.25 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
The clay's inertia is mR².
Use rotational inertias, not masses.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum is 0.9 m long. What is its period for small oscillations?

options.why: Correct. T = 2π√(L/g).
Take the square root.
The ratio is L/g.
Include 2π.

questions.stem: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 70 m. The coefficient of static friction is 0.8. What is the maximum speed without skidding?

options.why: Take the square root.
Correct. Static friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r.
Include the friction coefficient.
μ multiplies g r.

questions.stem: Masses of 6 kg and 1 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
Use T = m₂(g + a).
Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.

questions.stem: A 0.9 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 15$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: Include the 2π.
That is the frequency.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
The ratio is m/k.

questions.stem: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward at 3 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Include gravity.
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
Check the direction of the acceleration.

questions.stem: A 4 kg cart moving at 5 m/s collides with and sticks to a 2 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
The carts share the momentum.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.

questions.explanation: v_f = 4·5/6 = 3.33 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 16.7 J.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 9 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).
The exponent is 3/2.
Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).
T² ∝ r³.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 22 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its time of flight?

options.why: That is the time to the top; the flight is twice as long.
Use v₀ sin θ.
Use the vertical component.
Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 19.1 m/s, v₀y = 11 m/s. T = 2v₀y/g = 2.24 s.

questions.stem: A 5 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 8 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: I/R² = M/2.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
For a disk, I/R² = M/2.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 5.44 m/s².

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 10 m down a 20° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction removes energy.

questions.stem: A 5 kg ball moving at +4 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 3 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 3 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
That would be a sticking collision.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = 1 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 5 m/s.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 4 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 7 rad/s and amplitude 0.16 m. What is its speed when it is 0.016 m from equilibrium?

options.why: That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Use A² − x² under a square root.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.

questions.stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 1.5 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Some energy goes into rotation.
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ½MR².
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$3 \times 10^{25}$$ kg and radius $$8 \times 10^{6}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Potential energy uses 1/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Take the square root.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.

questions.stem: A 2 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 3t^2$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 4$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Integrate the force over time.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
Divide by the mass to get speed.
The force is not constant.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 64 N·s; v = J/m = 32 m/s.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = 1t^3 + 2t^2 - 5t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 2$$ s?

options.why: The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.
Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.

questions.explanation: a(t) = 6t + 4, so at t = 2 the value is 16.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 210$$ N/m is compressed 0.07 m and launches a 0.6 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
The ½ appears on both sides.
Take the square root.

questions.stem: A uniform 3 m beam weighing 100 N rests on supports at both ends. A 900 N load sits 1 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: The load is not at the center.
That is the left support's force.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 7 kg and radius 0.4 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it, 0.5 m from its center. What is its rotational inertia?

options.why: The axis is not through the center.
The parallel-axis term is Md².
Correct. Parallel-axis theorem: I = ½MR² + Md².
Include the disk's own I about its center.

questions.stem: A 2000 kg car heading east at 5 m/s collides with a 1000 kg car heading north at 13 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Weight each velocity by its mass.
Divide by the total mass.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 1x^3 - 30x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Take the square root.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 3x² − 30 = 0 gives x = 3.16 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.6 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
The weight acts at L/2.
τ = MgL/2.
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 5$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^3$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
The rod is not uniform.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.1 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.04$$ kg/s. What is its terminal speed?

options.why: Drag here is linear in v.
Solve mg = bv for v.
That is the time constant.
Correct. At terminal speed, mg = bv.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 24.5 m/s and τ = m/b = 2.5 s.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 5t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 5 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its position at $$t = 4$$ s?

options.why: Include the initial velocity.
That is the velocity.
Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.
Correct. Integrate twice, using the initial conditions.

questions.stem: A 22 g bullet moving at 220 m/s embeds in a 1.6 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
h = V²/(2g).
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.

questions.explanation: V = 2.98 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.454 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 4 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1.5 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.05 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
